one_liner: A U.S. Public Health Service officer (O-5) who runs healthcare risk management, incident reviews and patient-safety audits for ICE detention health services.
fit_summary: This posting is open only to commissioned USPHS officers and Call to Active Duty candidates, and it requires a healthcare credential (RN, NP/PA, or a healthcare administration field), an advanced degree, and years of healthcare quality experience. Nothing on file shows Daniel has a healthcare degree, a license, or a USPHS commission. Daniel's emergency-management consulting and policy knowledge are related to the work but do not meet these baseline requirements.
eligibility: Restricted: open only to USPHS Commissioned Corps officers and Call to Active Duty (CAD) candidates, not the general public, despite the 'public' hiring-path tag.
Must be a Registered Nurse, Nurse Practitioner/Physician Assistant, or in a Healthcare or Healthcare Administration related field, with a qualifying degree for the officer category.

Advanced degree (e.g., MPH, MA, MS) plus at least four years of relevant professional experience, including two years in public health program management, quality improvement, or risk management/compliance.
Certification in Healthcare Quality or Risk Management (CPHQ strongly recommended), or the ability to obtain it within one year.
Must maintain USPHS basic readiness, meet the physical demands (CPR, lifting, austere environments), and travel up to 30%.
keywords: data analysis for tracking, trending, and reporting
program development, review, implementation and evaluation
strategy: Confirm eligibility first. Unless you hold or are pursuing a USPHS commission with a qualifying healthcare degree, you cannot be selected, so don't spend time on this application.
If you ever want this kind of role, the path is long: a healthcare or health administration degree, an MPH or similar advanced degree, healthcare quality experience, and then a USPHS commission.
Redirect your effort to roles that fit what you have now, such as FEMA or DHS emergency management specialist, program analyst, or preparedness positions open to the public.
Also look at Virginia VDEM and Prince William County or Manassas emergency management jobs, and at legislative staff roles that use your policy knowledge and public-facing skills.

For those roles, frame your IEM work around specifics like [government clients served], [preparedness, recovery, or compliance tasks], and [deliverables], and list hours per week. Keep the resume within the two-page USAJOBS limit.
resume_bullets: Supported [client agency] emergency management and disaster recovery programs at IEM by [specific task, e.g., tracking compliance with grant or program requirements], working [hours/week] from [dates].
Analyzed [type of data, e.g., incident or recovery project data] to identify trends and drafted [reports or corrective recommendations] for [audience].
Coordinated with [number/type of stakeholders, e.g., state and local officials] to [specific outcome or activity], building working relationships across [organizations].
interview_questions: Describe how you conducted or supported a root cause analysis and turned the findings into a corrective action plan.
How would you monitor compliance with PBNDS, NCCHC, and ACA standards across facilities, including those not staffed by IHSC?
Tell us about a time you used data trends to drive a policy or practice change.
How do you handle sensitive inquiries raised by outside groups, such as NGOs, about detention conditions?
watch_outs: Status-only posting: USPHS officers and CAD candidates only. Daniel, as a civilian with no commission, is ineligible.
Requires a clinical or healthcare degree, an advanced degree, and risk management or quality certification, none of which are on file for Daniel.
The work involves heavy physical demands, austere detention settings, up to 30% travel, and possible 30-day TDYs.
The salary listing ($1–$150,000) is a placeholder; actual pay follows USPHS O-5 rank pay.
